q: Which mycobacterium does NOT cause tuberculosis?
e: M. bovis, M. africanum and M. microti belong to the M. tuberculosis complex. BCG, derived from M. bovis, can cause TB disease in some people (e.g. after intravesical BCG). M. avium-intracellulare is a non-tuberculous mycobacterium.

q: Which statement about TB epidemiology is FALSE?
o: TB is commoner in foreign-born US residents
MDR-TB makes up about 12% of US TB cases
TB incidence has fallen worldwide since 2000
e: MDR-TB was only about 1.2% of US cases in 2012. The book also states TB causes about 25% of deaths among people with HIV worldwide.

q: Which statement about genitourinary TB is FALSE?
o: Ascending spread is the commonest route
About 80% of GU TB involves the kidney
Sterile pyuria or haematuria is typical
e: Haematogenous seeding is by far the commonest route (lymphatic, direct inoculation, sexual and ascending spread also occur). Disease can be confined to the GU tract or disseminated. Untreated, it causes fibrosis, renal failure and infertility. Chronic prostatitis that persists despite several antibiotic courses is a common presentation.

q: Which is NOT a late complication of genitourinary TB?
e: Papulonecrotic tuberculid can appear early: a hypersensitivity skin reaction to disseminated antigen, culture- and usually PCR-negative. Late: infertility, scrotal fistula, autonephrectomy, contracted (thimble) bladder (commoner in developing countries) and ureteric strictures with a pipestem or beaded corkscrew appearance.

q: Which person is LEAST likely to have TB infection?
o: Fibrosis on chest film, TST 5 mm
Recent immigrant from Vietnam, TST 11 mm
e: CDC cut-offs: ≥5 mm for HIV, recent contacts, fibrotic changes on CXR and immunosuppression; ≥10 mm for recent immigrants from high-burden countries, drug users, high-risk settings and young children; ≥15 mm for people with no risk factors. A BCG-vaccinated person likely comes from a high-incidence country, so 10 mm applies. (The book's key also lists 'HIV with TST 3 mm' as likely infected, which is below the 5 mm cut-off.) Local cut-offs may vary.

q: Which result most specifically diagnoses genitourinary TB?
e: Gold standard: positive AFB culture of urine or tissue; first-voided morning urine is the best sample (several samples are usually sent). Nucleic acid amplification or granulomas on histology support the diagnosis. All patients need a chest X-ray to exclude infectious pulmonary TB.

q: Which statement about imaging in GU TB is FALSE?
o: IVU is best for early renal changes
MRI is often used to diagnose GU TB
CT helps most when disease is extensive
Calcification is the commonest plain-film sign
e: MRI is not sufficiently better than CT or IVU to be used often. The commonest IVU finding is obstructive uropathy from scarring. The choice of test depends on the site of disease.

q: Which statement about anti-TB drugs is TRUE?
e: Ethambutol's main toxicity is ocular (reduced acuity, red–green colour blindness). Start with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol (standard course: 2 months of all four, then 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin). Streptomycin is not hepatotoxic and is not first-line in the US. Rifampin resistance is a surrogate marker for MDR-TB. Relapse occurs in up to 22%, so follow up.

q: Of these drugs, which is most likely still active against XDR-TB?
e: Book definition: XDR-TB is resistant to isoniazid, rifampin, any fluoroquinolone and at least one injectable (e.g. amikacin). Since 2021 WHO defines XDR-TB as MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to a fluoroquinolone and to bedaquiline or linezolid ('pre-XDR' is MDR plus fluoroquinolone resistance).

q: Which urological intervention in GU TB is needed emergently?
o: Boari flap for a lower ureteric stricture
Augmentation of a small contracted bladder
e: Other operations are best done 4–6 weeks after starting drugs, letting inflammation settle, bacillary load fall and lesions stabilise. Indications: relieve obstruction, drain infection, remove a non-functioning infected kidney resisting cure, treat hypertension from an excluded kidney, reconstruct (balloon dilation and stenting of strictures, Boari flap, augmentation).

q: Which statement about S. haematobium is TRUE?
o: Cercariae enter via skin, becoming schistosomules
Biomphalaria snails are its intermediate hosts
Adult worms cause most of the tissue damage
Adult worms penetrate the skin to start infection
e: Bulinus snails host S. haematobium; Biomphalaria hosts S. mansoni and Oncomelania S. japonicum (Helix and Achatina are land snails). Most pathology comes from the host immune response to eggs. Eggs have a terminal spine; adults live mainly in the perivesical venous plexus, on average 3–5 years (some for decades).

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Praziquantel is the only WHO-approved treatment
Acute schistosomiasis is called Katayama fever
About 1.1 billion have active S. haematobium
Urine egg counts are the first-line gold standard
e: About 1 billion people are at risk, but about 112 million are actively infected with S. haematobium. Katayama fever is named after a valley in Japan once endemic for S. japonicum. PCR and serology are sensitive but not first-line; cystoscopy with biopsy or rectal biopsy is for difficult cases or suspected cancer. Egg excretion peaks around midday, so midday urine samples are preferred. Praziquantel (usually 40 mg/kg) is the drug of choice.

q: Which is NOT a recognised feature of urogenital schistosomiasis?
e: Ureteric strictures are usually distal, with hydronephrosis. Other features: golf-hole or stenotic ureteric orifices, chronic schistosomal ulcers that can bleed, epidermisation and adenoid (goblet-cell) metaplasia, and rectosigmoid polyposis. Squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest associated bladder cancer; the book says these are usually well differentiated or verrucous with a relatively good prognosis.

q: Which is NOT used to reconstruct schistosomal ureteric lesions?
e: Less morbid options suffice (also suprapubic intravesical ureterostomy). The book reserves autotransplantation for other settings (it cites multiple or large renal tumours).

q: Which statement about lymphatic filariasis is FALSE?
o: Most infected people have no symptoms at all
W. bancrofti causes about 90% of human LF
Wolbachia endosymbionts live in the worms
Chronic LF mostly affects short-term visitors
e: Transmission is inefficient, so chronic disease needs years of repeated bites and is seen mostly in long-term residents. Killing Wolbachia with doxycycline reduces microfilaria release and larval moulting. W. bancrofti causes chyluria, filarial hydrocele and occasionally severe scrotal and penile lymphoedema; obstruction follows repeated reinfection.

q: Which drug must be avoided in onchocerciasis or heavy Loa loa microfilaraemia?
e: DEC can cause blindness in onchocerciasis (inflammation in the anterior chamber) and encephalopathy with heavy Loa loa infection. About 99% of people with onchocerciasis live in sub-Saharan Africa.

q: A renal hydatid cyst is being removed. The main specific intraoperative danger is:
e: Echinococcosis can form renal cysts; rupture or spillage at surgery can cause anaphylaxis.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
e: The innate response is rapid and less specific; the adaptive response adds specificity and memory. The two usually work together.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Neutrophils present peptide on MHC class II
Neutrophils cannot kill by oxidative bursts
Macrophages are the first cells to meet BCG
CD8 T cells are the first cells to meet BCG
e: BCG also binds directly to urothelium. Macrophages and neutrophils both kill oxidatively and migrate along chemokine gradients; only macrophages present antigen on MHC class II. (The book also says only macrophages ingest pathogens; neutrophils are phagocytes too.)

q: Which statement about cytokines is TRUE?
o: IL-12 is the principal Th1 cytokine
Interferon α has no role in BCG response
IL-4, IL-5 and IL-10 are Th1 cytokines
IL-8 drives naive T cells to make IL-4
e: Th1: IL-12, interferon γ, IL-2 and TNF-α; drives viral clearance and antitumour immunity. Th2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-10 and IL-13; linked with chronic inflammation, inhibits antitumour responses; urinary Th2 cytokines after BCG predict a worse outcome. IL-8 is a chemokine (attracts neutrophils).

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: CD8 T cells evolved to kill virus-infected cells
Regulatory T cells are a subset of the CD8 T cells
CD4 helper cells have a single phenotype
B cells are named after the bone marrow source
e: CD8 cells can kill almost any target, even chemoresistant cells. Tregs are CD4+ and inhibit adaptive responses. 'B' comes from the bursa of Fabricius in chickens. CD4 phenotypes include Th1, Th2, Tregs and others.

q: The main function of B cells is to:
o: Make anti-BCG antibodies that help BCG
e: Memory B cells give faster, stronger secondary responses. Anti-BCG antibodies are probably harmful, clearing BCG faster and weakening the antitumour effect.

q: The three stages of the immune editing hypothesis, in order, are:
e: Early tumours can be recognised and eliminated; clinically evident tumours must escape immune recognition.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: There are no data linking inflammation to prostate
Charred meat is linked to prostatic inflammation
Inflammation data are strongest in kidney cancer
Schistosomiasis rarely causes squamous bladder cancer
e: The strongest link is bladder cancer: chronic schistosomiasis leads to squamous cell carcinoma. Prostate cancer may also be driven by chronic inflammation, though its cause is undefined.

q: A dense CD8 T-cell infiltrate is associated with:
o: A worse prognosis in bladder cancer
No prognostic value in any GU cancer
A worse prognosis in kidney cancer
A better prognosis in kidney cancer
e: In kidney cancer there is an active CD8 response, yet more CD8 cells paradoxically predict worse outcome; in bladder cancer a strong CD8 infiltrate predicts better outcome.

q: BCG's antitumour effect in NMIBC is mediated by all EXCEPT:
e: Th2 CD4 cells are associated with worse outcome. BCG stimulates both innate and adaptive immunity and is the prototype of successful cancer immunotherapy.

q: Which statement about PD-1 is TRUE?
o: PD-1 binding PD-L1 exhausts CD8 T cells
PD-1 is an intracellular cell-cycle protein
PD-1 binding drives interferon γ release
PD-1 signals PD-L1 to kill the tumour cell
e: Immune checkpoints are cell-surface proteins that dampen CD8 effector function when bound by their ligands. Blocking PD-1/PD-L1 restores function and shrinks tumours in a minority. Other checkpoints include CTLA-4 and LAG-3 (the book writes 'LAG-4'). The PD-1 pathway normally limits autoimmunity.

q: Which is an FDA-approved vaccine for a GU cancer?
o: Gardasil as a bladder cancer vaccine
e: Sipuleucel-T targets prostatic acid phosphatase in asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic metastatic CRPC (IMPACT trial). Other phase III vaccines in kidney and prostate cancer failed. Vaccines are well tolerated but give few objective responses.

q: Which statement is TRUE (per the chapter)?
o: Complete responses are frequent in most patients
Response rates are under 10% in bladder cancer
Benefit is seen only when combined with chemotherapy
e: Overall response is about 20–25%. Pembrolizumab improved overall survival versus second-line chemotherapy (KEYNOTE-045), though not progression-free survival (the book says both). It is also active first-line in cisplatin-ineligible patients; PD-L1 expression may predict response. Newer standards include avelumab maintenance and enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab first-line. In prostate cancer, PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy has no robust activity.

q: First-line nivolumab plus ipilimumab in clear cell RCC:
o: Is less toxic than a single checkpoint drug
e: CheckMate 214: better overall and progression-free survival than sunitinib, but more toxic, with endocrine adverse events fairly common. Anti-PD-1 also works second-line in RCC.

q: In previously treated clear cell RCC, which drug improved overall survival with fewer severe side effects than everolimus?
e: CheckMate 025 (Motzer, 2015). Loss-of-function PBRM1 mutations were associated with benefit from anti-PD-1 therapy in metastatic ccRCC.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology; Ch 61

q: Which statement about DNA is FALSE?
o: A purine pairs with a pyrimidine
Its sugar is ribose, as in RNA
e: DNA's sugar is 2-deoxyribose; RNA uses ribose and uracil instead of thymine. Phosphate–sugar links form the backbone; the double helix is held by hydrogen bonds; A–T is weaker than G–C.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Transcription makes mRNA in the nucleus
Translation converts DNA into linear RNA
Proteins are made only inside the nucleus
e: mRNA carries the code to the cytoplasm, where translation makes protein. Transcription is regulated by DNA response elements (in promoters or enhancers) that bind nuclear proteins, so genes sharing consensus sequences respond together; it is not controlled by binding to mRNA sequences. Alternative splicing includes or excludes exons, making several isoforms from one gene, a tightly regulated process.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement about translation is TRUE?
o: Each amino acid has only one codon
e: The code is redundant, so different sequences can give the same protein (a polymorphism), though some change an amino acid. Frameshifts are the most damaging mutations. The book calls the nuclear matrix the site of mRNA transcription; its protein make-up is tissue- and state-specific (the basis of markers such as NMP22).
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Inhibiting the proteasome speeds cancer growth
Protein disposal is an active, regulated process
Tagged proteins are degraded in the proteasome
e: Perturbed ubiquitination is common in cancer, so inhibiting it (e.g. proteasome inhibitors) is a promising therapy. The proteasome is cylindrical.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Oncogenes arise by silencing a proto-oncogene
Oncogenes are always caused by retroviruses
e: Three routes: activating mutation, amplification and chromosomal rearrangement. Tumour suppressors restrain growth and are lost by homozygous deletion, loss of one allele plus mutation or epigenetic silencing of the other, or mutation of both; some escape the two-hit rule (dominant negative, haploinsufficiency). Deletion is the abnormality most linked to tumour suppressor loss; amplification and double minutes raise oncogene copy number.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement about DNA methylation is TRUE?
o: It occurs on cytosine in CpG pairs
It changes the DNA base sequence directly
It marks proteins for ubiquitin tagging
e: Promoter CpG island methylation silences genes (e.g. tumour suppressors in cancer); loss of normal methylation can switch on oncogenes. 5-methylcytosine can deaminate to thymine, causing C→T transitions.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: VHL causes clear cell RCC and phaeochromocytoma
VHL predisposes to papillary type RCC
e: VHL: clear cell RCC, retinal angiomas, phaeochromocytomas, CNS haemangioblastomas, epididymal cystadenomas, pancreatic islet tumours (not papillary RCC, adrenocortical or epididymal carcinoma). Germline genes may also act in sporadic disease (VHL in ccRCC).
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement about ELAC2, MSR1 and RNASEL is TRUE?
o: Only RNASEL is a proven prostate cancer gene
They are the strongest GWAS risk regions
All are proven causes of prostate cancer
e: They were linked by family linkage and some case-control studies. GWAS (high-density SNP arrays) most consistently implicate the 8q24 region across racial groups.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Cyclin–cdk complexes dephosphorylate RB1 at G1/S
Main checkpoints are at G1/S and G2/M
G2/M checkpoints mainly sense nutrient supply
INK4 proteins mainly inhibit cyclin B–cdc2
e: Cyclin–cdk complexes phosphorylate RB1 (and p107, p130), releasing E2F, which pairs with DP1/DP2 to drive replication genes. INK4 proteins block cyclin D–cdk4/6. Hypoxia, nutrients and cytokines act at G1/S; DNA damage triggers arrest at both. Cyclins rise and fall phase-specifically, making the cycle ordered and irreversible. RB1 mutations are common in urological cancers.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement about TP53 is TRUE?
o: It is a rarely mutated gene in cancer
Its apoptosis acts mainly via CD95
It triggers arrest, repair or death
e: TP53 responds to DNA damage by arresting the cycle via CDKN1A (p21) and inducing repair genes; if repair fails it triggers apoptosis via APAF-1/caspase 9. It is the most commonly mutated gene in cancer. Most testicular germ cell tumours keep wild-type TP53 and intact DNA damage responses, explaining their cure with DNA-damaging drugs.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which pairing is correct?
o: Base excision repair: UV light damage
e: BER: deamination, radiation, oxidative stress, alkylating agents. MMR: polymerase mispairs. Double-strand breaks (ionising radiation, free radicals, chemicals): homologous recombination (uses the sister chromatid) or non-homologous end joining. BRCA1/BRCA2 work in HR with RAD51 and BARD1, recruited by PCNA. Inherited repair defects raise cancer risk.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement about apoptosis is FALSE?
o: Bcl-2 itself inhibits the mitochondrial pathway
e: Procaspases are activated by proteolytic cleavage, starting a cascade from initiator to executioner caspases. Intrinsic pathway: Bcl-2 family controls cytochrome c release. Extrinsic: death receptors. Because TP53 is mutated in over half of cancers, TP53-independent (ligand-dependent) apoptosis is an attractive target. Bcl-2 is overexpressed in some GU cancers. Ceramide and clusterin are possible modulators.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement is FALSE?
e: No strong link to methylation is known. Telomeres are repetitive non-coding caps lost with division and oxidative damage. The length checkpoint (TP53, RB1) causes senescence or apoptosis; if it fails, chromosomal instability promotes cancer. Most cancers and premalignant lesions have short telomeres and express telomerase, a therapeutic target.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which rearrangement is NOT typical of a GU cancer?
e: BCR–ABL is CML. TMPRSS2–ERG fusion (intrachromosomal deletion) occurs in about 50% of prostate cancers; isochromosome 8q with 8p loss in some prostate cancers; MiT/TFE translocation RCC; chromosome 9 loss in urothelial cancer (part of the FISH bladder test). Testis tumours carry isochromosome 12p, the GU cancer most tied to a karyotypic change. Chromosomal chaos correlates with aggressiveness.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Urine is proven sterile in healthy adults
e: RNA-seq unbiasedly detects microRNAs, non-coding RNAs, fusions and overexpression. Urine has its own microbiota, previously missed by culture; urinary and gut microbiomes may influence GU cancers and treatment response or toxicity.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: De novo high-grade cancers are luminal
Cancer stem cells form most of a tumour
e: De novo high-grade bladder cancers are basal-like. Stem cells can differentiate along several lineages and are immortal; cancer may be a stem cell disease in which a small stem-cell population maintains the tumour, so targeting it might eradicate cancer.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology

q: Which finding best supports a gene being a disease-relevant oncogene or tumour suppressor?
o: High expression in normal tissue only
Copy change plus an other-allele hit
Normal copy number in every tumour
A single polymorphism near the gene
e: Copy-number alterations in a gene coupled with changes in the other allele are evidence of a disease-relevant role. Most solid tumours show numerical and structural chromosome changes with intratumoural variation.
s: Ch 62 Molecular genetics and cancer biology
